fact: Aberdeen Street was originally called William Street in old Bowronville before being renamed, probably after the Scottish city.
Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Boulevard honors Harlem's pastor and congressman, the first Black New Yorker elected to Congress. His stretch of 7th Avenue was renamed in 1974.
Adelphi Street was named for London's Adelphi Terrace, built by the Adam brothers between 1768 and 1772.
Ainslie Street honors Justice James Ainslie, a Williamsburg trustee in the 1830s. The street was officially opened and paved in 1850.
Alabama Avenue is part of a cluster of state named streets in East New York, southern states in one section, northeastern in another.
Albany Avenue was named in 1835 as a tribute to the Erie Canal, seven Crown Heights avenues trace a path up the Hudson and along the canal.
Albemarle Road was just plain 'Avenue A' until 1897, when developers renamed it after a London street to give Flatbush a more refined English feel.
Named for William Henry Allen, a U.S. naval officer and hero of the War of 1812.
Amboy Road is named for Perth Amboy, the New Jersey city it pointed toward via the Tottenville ferry. Amboy itself comes from the Lenape word Ompoge, meaning level ground.
Amersfort Place recalls Nieuw Amersfoort, the Dutch name for Flatlands before the British renamed it in 1664.
Amherst Street starts Manhattan Beach's A to P alphabetical grid of English place names, laid out when the area was an exclusive 1870s seaside resort.
Amity Street takes its name from the English word for 'friendship.' The street was developed beginning in the 1840s with Greek Revival rowhouses.
Amsterdam Avenue was renamed from 10th Avenue in 1890 for the Dutch city of Amsterdam, a nod to the New Amsterdam roots of the whole island.
Named after Ann White, wife of merchant Captain Thomas White, because other merchants' wives already had streets named for them.
Argyle Road's name comes from Argyll in western Scotland. Developers chose British place names to market the area as a refined residential enclave.
Arion Place was renamed from Wall Street to honor Bushwick's famous German singing society, the 1886 hall is now loft apartments.
Arlington Avenue likely takes its name from Arlington, Virginia, the former Lee estate turned national cemetery after the Civil War.
Arthur Kill Road is named for the Arthur Kill, the tidal strait it parallels. The name is an anglicization of the Dutch achter kill, meaning back channel, the waterway behind Staten Island.
Ascan Avenue honors Ascan Backus, a German born farmer known as the King Farmer of Long Island. His son cut the road in 1909 and named it for him.
The street was renamed to distance it from the jail's grim reputation. The name 'Ashland' likely honors Henry Clay's Kentucky estate, following a widespread 19th century naming pattern.
Named for John Jacob Astor, once the richest person in America, who built his fortune starting with beaver fur.
Astoria Park South runs along the southern edge of Astoria Park, the East River green space beneath the Hell Gate and Triborough bridges.
Atlantic Avenue was named for the Atlantic Ocean and became one of Brooklyn's major east west commercial corridors.

Audubon Avenue honors John James Audubon, the naturalist and painter of Birds of America, whose estate Minnie's Land covered this part of Washington Heights. He is buried a few blocks away at Trinity Cemetery.
Autumn Avenue used to be Railroad Avenue, named for the nearby LIRR station before getting its seasonal rename.
Avenue A belongs to the simple lettered naming system that organized much of the East Village and Alphabet City.
Avenue B continues the alphabetized street system that gave Alphabet City its modern nickname.
Avenue C is part of the East Village's alphabetized avenue system, a simple naming scheme that became a neighborhood identity.
Avenue D marks the eastern edge of the alphabetized avenue system closest to the East River.
Baltic Street sits between Atlantic Ave and Pacific Street, all three named for bodies of water in Brooklyn's maritime heyday.
Banker Street preserves another local family name inside Greenpoint's waterfront era street grid.
Barbey Street is named for developer Andrew Barbey, his partner Sackman got a street too, about a mile to the west.
Named for Reverend Henry Barclay, who became the second rector of Trinity Church in 1746.
Bath Avenue is named for Bath, England, developer B.J. Osborne wanted his 1850s seaside colony to feel just as refined.
Battery Avenue is named for the gun batteries at Fort Hamilton, until 1898 locals could freely stroll right into the fort.
Originally Orange Street at the heart of the Five Points slum, renamed in 1853 for Lt. Col. Charles Baxter, killed in the Mexican-American War.

Bay Parkway was originally 22nd Avenue, officially renamed by the New York State legislature on May 17, 1892, to integrate it into a scenic parkway network inspired by Olmsted and Vaux's vision for Brooklyn.
Bay Ridge Avenue takes its name from the Bay Ridge neighborhood, originally called Yellow Hook by Dutch settlers for its yellowish clay soil.
Bay Street is named for Upper New York Bay, whose shore it follows from the St. George ferry landing toward the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. It has been the island's front door since steam ferry days.
Bayard Street honors the powerful Bayard family, Nicholas Bayard was Stuyvesant's nephew and became NYC mayor in 1685.
Not named for a beach. It's a corruption of "Bache," for Paul Bache, son in law of landowner Anthony Lispenard.
Beadel Street is named for the Beadel family, who held large portions of land in the area during the mid 1850s.
Beard Street honors William Beard, an Irish immigrant who built the Erie Basin and transformed Red Hook into a major shipping hub.
Originally Bever Graft (Beaver Canal) in Dutch New Amsterdam, named for the beaver pelts that were the colony's chief currency.
Bedell Lane is named for the Bedell family, among Canarsie's founding families whose descendants lived in the area from colonial times.
Named for the colonial village of Bedford, a 17th century Dutch settlement at today's Bedford Avenue and Fulton Street.
Beekman Street preserves the name of the Beekman family, one of the elite colonial dynasties that stamped themselves onto Manhattan's map.
Bell Boulevard is named for Abraham Bell, a Quaker whose 1824 farm became the heart of Bayside. The old lane split his land into an upper and a lower farm.
Named for August Belmont, the Wall Street titan who founded the Belmont Stakes and changed his name from Schonberg to sound more French.
Bennett Avenue honors James Gordon Bennett, founder of the New York Herald, whose Washington Heights estate became Bennett Park, the highest natural point in Manhattan.
Benson Avenue takes its name from the Benson family whose farmland became Bensonhurst. Arthur W.
Bergen Street honors a Norwegian ship's carpenter who sailed to New Amsterdam in 1633 and became one of Brooklyn's founding settlers.
Named for philosopher George Berkeley, same guy Berkeley, California is named after. He pronounced it 'BARK-lee.'
Berrian Boulevard honors the Berrien family. In 1727 Cornelius Berrien bought an East River island off Astoria for the family homestead, later filled in to become the mainland the boulevard crosses.
William Berriman was a newspaper man whose buddy, a local Democratic boss, got a Brooklyn street named after him.
Berry Street is named for John Berry and belongs to the northward extension of Williamsburg's 19th century street grid.
Named for Joanna Graham Bethune, a philanthropist who cofounded the New York Orphan Asylum with Mrs. Alexander Hamilton.
Originally just 'Avenue B,' developers gave it the posh English name Beverley in 1897 to sell more houses nearby.
Bleecker Street is named for Anthony Lispenard Bleecker, a banker, merchant, and member of a prominent old New York family.
Boerum Place honors Simon Boerum, a Brooklyn farmer turned Continental Congress delegate who helped defeat the Galloway Plan in 1774.
Boerum Street recalls Jacob Boerum, who farmed 58 acres in Williamsburg, his land was later sold to developers who built homes for German settlers.
Bogart Street is named for a 1650s Dutch settler, and yes, actor Humphrey Bogart was his direct descendant through seven generations.
Bond Street likely takes its name from Manhattan's Bond Street, itself possibly named for London's famous shopping street.
Named from the Dutch bouwerij, meaning farm; it began as the road to Peter Stuyvesant's farm.
Bowne Street honors John Bowne, the Quaker whose 1662 arrest for hosting worship in his Flushing home led to a landmark defense of religious freedom in America.
Bragg Street is named for F. S. Bragg, one of the surveyors who literally drew the Sheepshead Bay street grid for Kings County in the 1870s.
Brevoort Place recalls the Dutch Brevoort family, who took their name from the village of Bredevoort, meaning 'broad ford', in the Netherlands.
Originally Brugh Straat in Dutch, named for bridges spanning the Heere Gracht canal along present day Broad Street.
Brigham Street is named for E. D. Brigham, a surveyor who mapped out this part of Sheepshead Bay's street grid in the 1870s.
Bristol Street was originally part of Baltic Street, renamed in 1887 when the New Lots Board of Trade reorganized 67 street names.
Named for the Heere Gracht, a Dutch canal that ran down its center before being filled in 1676.
From the Dutch Brede weg (broad way); it traces the old Wickquasgeck trail used by Native Americans long before the grid.
Brooklyn Avenue is part of Crown Heights' Erie Canal tribute, avenues named in 1835 for cities along the canal route.
Named for John Broome, a Revolutionary War militia colonel who became New York's lieutenant governor in 1804.
Likely named for poet William Cullen Bryant, whose famous poem 'Thanatopsis' on death echoes through nearby Cypress Hills Cemetery.
Developer Dean Alvord gave this street its English name in 1899 to make his Prospect Park South subdivision feel like a country estate.
Named in 1835 to honor the Erie Canal, seven Crown Heights avenues trace the canal route from Kingston to Buffalo.
Named for the Dutch settlement 'Boswijck', town in the woods, chartered by Peter Stuyvesant in 1661. It became a mansion lined boulevard for brewers.
Butler Street likely honors Benjamin Franklin Butler, the New York lawyer who served as U.S. Attorney General under Jackson and Van Buren and cofounded NYU.
Cabrini Boulevard honors Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini, the first United States citizen to be made a saint. The former Northern Avenue was renamed for her in 1939, two years after her death.
Cadman Plaza honors S. Parkes Cadman, a Brooklyn pastor whose 1920s radio sermons reached millions, America's first 'radio minister.'
Cadman Plaza honors S. Parkes Cadman, a Brooklyn pastor whose 1920s radio sermons reached millions, America's first 'radio minister.'
Named for Vice President John C. Calhoun, who infamously called slavery a 'positive good', many Calhoun streets nationwide have been renamed.
Calyer Street preserves one of the family names embedded in Greenpoint's 19th century street grid.
Named for the actual canal dug here in the early 1800s to drain the polluted Collect Pond.
Canarsie Road takes its name from the Canarsie band of the Lenape, who inhabited southeastern Brooklyn.
While many nearby streets were named by Trinity Church for rectors and wardens, the specific origin of the Carlisle name is not well documented in available historical sources.
Fort Greene's streets, Carlton, Adelphi, Cumberland, Portland, were all named after fashionable Westminster terraces in 19th century London.
Carroll Street honors the only Catholic signer of the Declaration of Independence, whose Maryland troops fought at the Battle of Brooklyn.
Catherine Street honors Catherine Rutgers, her grandson Henry gave his name to a certain New Jersey university.
Named for the Caton family, Susan Martense Caton's mansion once stood right at Flatbush and Caton Avenues.
Caton Place is named for the same family as Caton Avenue, the prosperous Catons of old Flatbush.
Like many early Brooklyn streets, Cedar Street was likely named for the cedar trees that once grew in the area.
Centre Street in Brooklyn takes its name from its position near the center of the old village of Brooklyn.
Chambers Street honors John Chambers, a colonial lawyer and New York politician.
Channel Avenue in Gerritsen Beach is named for the tidal waterways and channels that define the neighborhood's coastal geography.
Chapel Street in downtown Brooklyn likely takes its name from an early church or chapel that once stood nearby.
Named after Charles Christopher Amos, who inherited the old Admiral Peter Warren estate the street passed through.
Chauncey Avenue honors Commodore Isaac Chauncey (1779 to 1840), who commanded U.S. naval forces on Lake Ontario during the War of 1812.
Chauncey Street honors a War of 1812 naval commodore who commanded all American forces on Lake Ontario at just age 40.
Cheever Place honors Samuel Cheever, one of three commissioners who laid out the street grid in Cobble Hill.
Cherry Street in Brooklyn shares its name with Manhattan's famous Cherry Street, both likely named for cherry orchards that once dotted the area.
Chester Avenue in Brooklyn is part of a cluster of streets likely named after Chester, the historic walled city in England.
Chester Street in Brownsville is likely named after the English city of Chester, following Brooklyn's tradition of borrowing British place names.
Chestnut Avenue in Midwood is named for the chestnut trees that once grew throughout Brooklyn's landscape.
Chestnut Street in East New York is named for the American chestnut trees that once flourished across Brooklyn before blight wiped them out.
Christopher Avenue runs through Brownsville and is likely named after a local landowner or developer from Brooklyn's early growth period.
Named for Charles Christopher Amos, the same landowner who gave his first name to nearby Charles Street.
Chrystie Street is named for John Chrystie, a physician and landowner whose family held property in this part of Manhattan.
Church Avenue is named for the Flatbush Reformed Dutch Church, whose congregation dates to 1654 under Peter Stuyvesant.
Named for Trinity Church, the historic Anglican parish founded in 1697 that once owned vast tracts of Lower Manhattan.
Clarendon Road was created when Brooklyn's lettered avenues east of Flatbush Avenue were renamed in the 1890s.
Clark Street runs through Brooklyn Heights, where most streets are named after early landowners who subdivided their farms into building lots in the early 1800s.
Clarkson Avenue in Flatbush was named for a local Clarkson family landowner from before the area's streets were formally laid out.
Named for General Matthew Clarkson, a Revolutionary War soldier who served as aide to Benedict Arnold before Arnold's defection.
Classon Avenue gets its name from the Dutch patronymic 'Claeson' meaning 'son of Claes', pure old New Amsterdam heritage.
Claver Place was renamed from Ormond Place to honor St. Peter Claver, a Jesuit priest who spent 40 years fighting the slave trade in Colombia.
Clay Street in Greenpoint was originally 'C Street' in an alphabetical grid, later possibly named for Senator Henry Clay or a local 17th century pirate.
Clermont Avenue is named after Robert Fulton's pioneering steamboat, the Clermont, which revolutionized travel between Brooklyn and Manhattan.
Formerly Marion Street, renamed in 1908 to honor President Grover Cleveland after his death that year.
Cleveland Street honors the only U.S. president to serve two nonconsecutive terms. He was also a former New York governor.
Clifford Place is a small street in Brooklyn whose exact namesake has been lost to time.
Clifton Place in Clinton Hill was likely named after the English place name Clifton, meaning 'settlement on a cliff,' following Brooklyn's British naming tradition.
Clinton Avenue was named for DeWitt Clinton, the NYS governor who championed the Erie Canal, his mansion lined street became Brooklyn's 'Gold Coast.'
Clinton Street is named for DeWitt Clinton, the powerful New York politician most associated with the Erie Canal era.
Clove Road takes its name from the Dutch word 'kloven' meaning cleft. It once followed a valley between two hills in Crown Heights.
Clymer Street in Williamsburg is named for George Clymer of Pennsylvania, one of only six men to sign both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
Coffey Street in Red Hook was renamed in 1891 for Alderman Michael J. Coffey, 'the Emperor of Red Hook,' whose political grip was so strong the area was called Coffeyville.
Coleman Street in Marine Park is likely named for a local landowner or developer but its specific namesake is not well documented.
Coleridge Street in Manhattan Beach is part of an alphabetical set of English themed street names, likely honoring poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge.
Coles Street in Carroll Gardens was named for Jordan Coles, a schools commissioner who owned several tide mills in the area.
College Place in Brooklyn Heights was named for the Brooklyn Collegiate Institute for Young Ladies, a girls' school that stood nearby in the 1830s.
College Point Boulevard is named for the College Point neighborhood, which took its name from St. Paul's College, an Episcopal school founded on the point in the 1830s.
Named for Thomas Collister, who served as sexton of Trinity Church from 1790 to 1816.
Colonial Road in Bay Ridge was just First Avenue until early 1900s real estate speculators gave it a fancier name to attract buyers.
Columbia Place in Brooklyn Heights takes its name from Christopher Columbus, like many 'Columbia' streets laid out in the early republic era.
Columbia Street honors Christopher Columbus. The name dates to the pre Revolutionary era when Brooklyn Heights was considered as a seat of government.
Columbus Place in Bedford-Stuyvesant is named for explorer Christopher Columbus, reflecting the 19th century practice of honoring historical figures in Brooklyn street names.
Named for the businesses that fled here during Manhattan's 1798 yellow fever epidemic.
Commercial Street in Greenpoint was named for the bustling waterfront commerce that defined the neighborhood, from glassworks to shipbuilding.
Concord Street in Downtown Brooklyn is named for the Massachusetts town where the first shots of the American Revolution were fired in April 1775.
Conduit Boulevard is named for the underground brick aqueduct that once carried water from Long Island to Brooklyn's Ridgewood Reservoir.
Coney Island Avenue leads to Coney Island, whose name comes from the Dutch 'Konijn Eiland' meaning Rabbit Island. The Lenape called it Narrioch, 'land without shadows.'
Congress Street in Cobble Hill is believed to be named for the U.S. Congress, part of Brooklyn's tradition of patriotic street naming in the early republic.
Conklin Avenue in Canarsie was the neighborhood's original commercial center. It predates the numbered street grid and was named for an early local developer.
Named after a Dutch colonial family, Conover Street in Red Hook traces back to 1757 landowner John Conover whose name is the same old Dutch name as Kowenhoven.
Convent Avenue is named for the Convent of the Sacred Heart, a Catholic academy that stood on the bluff here in the mid 1800s.
Cook Street preserves an older local family name inside Williamsburg's rapidly urbanized street grid.
Cooper Street honors industrialist Peter Cooper, who ran a glue factory nearby and later founded Cooper Union for free education.
Originally named for anti Semitic railroad baron Austin Corbin, this Brighton Beach street was rebranded as M. Corbin Place to honor Revolutionary War heroine Margaret Corbin.
Cornelia Street is named for Cornelia Herring, granddaughter of Dutch settler Robert Herring, on whose farm the street was laid out in 1794.
Corona Avenue is named for the Corona neighborhood. Developers used the Latin word for crown to advertise the area as the crown of Queens communities.
Cortelyou Road honors Jacques Cortelyou, a 17th century French Huguenot surveyor who founded the settlement that became New Utrecht in 1657.
Manhattan's longest true alley, laid out in 1817 and named for the prominent Dutch colonial Van Cortlandt family.
Named for Oloff Van Cortlandt, a Dutch colonial brewer and burgomaster of New Amsterdam from 1655 to 1666.
Court Street takes its name from the courthouses and civic institutions of downtown Brooklyn, a functional name for the county's administrative core.
Coventry Road in East Flatbush is part of a tiny enclave of English named streets created by 19th century developers who replaced the old lettered avenues.
Covert Street likely honors the Covert family, early Dutch settlers of Brooklyn whose patriarch Teunis Jans Covert emigrated from Holland in 1651.
One of Brooklyn Heights' famous 'fruit streets,' Cranberry Street was likely named by the Hicks brothers, early landowners who sold exotic fruits.
Originally opened as Grinnell Street in 1835, this Red Hook street was renamed in 1891 for Joseph M. Creamer, a Brooklyn police surgeon.
Crescent Street takes its name from its curving path. In Astoria, 19th century maps show a bent road called The Crescent that still throws the street off the grid between 30th and 34th Avenues.
Crooke Avenue honors Philip Schuyler Crooke, a Civil War brigadier general, U.S. Congressman, and longtime Flatbush resident who lived in a historic Dutch farmhouse.
Cropsey Avenue is named for a family of German immigrants whose descendants included Hudson River School painter Jasper Cropsey.
Named for William Bedlow Crosby, a 19th century millionaire who inherited hundreds of SoHo acres from Henry Rutgers.
Cross Bay Boulevard is named for its route, the only road that crosses Jamaica Bay, linking mainland Queens to the Rockaway peninsula over water and marsh.
Crown Street gave its name to Crown Heights when it was extended in 1916, replacing the old neighborhood name 'Crow Hill' with something more aspirational.
Cumberland Street in Fort Greene was named after Cumberland Terrace in Westminster, London, as part of a pattern of giving Brooklyn streets fashionable English names.
Named for the cypress trees that once blanketed the hills of eastern Brooklyn, the same trees that gave Cypress Hills Cemetery its name in 1848.
Cypress Hills Street takes its name from the Cypress Hills neighborhood, itself named for the tall cypress trees growing on local hills and the Cypress Hills Cemetery established in 1848.
Dahill Road's name Dahill derives from the Gaelic O Dathaill, an Irish family from County Roscommon. Some Dahills arrived in New York in 1866, but the street did not receive its name until the 1920s.
Dahlgren Place honors the 'father of American naval ordnance'. The city once misspelled his street sign as 'Dahlgreen' until Bay Ridge residents demanded a fix.
Dean Street honors Silas Deane, America's first diplomat to France, who helped recruit foreign volunteers for the Revolution but died disgraced on a ship bound for home.
DeBevoise Avenue preserves another old Brooklyn family name in the interior Williamsburg and Bushwick grid.
Debevoise Street commemorates Charles Debevoise, a village schoolmaster. The family name itself means 'Beautiful Road' in French.
Decatur Street is named for Stephen Decatur Jr., who at 25 became the youngest captain in U.S. Navy history after his daring raid in Tripoli harbor.
Degraw Street is named after James De Graw, an early Brooklyn landowner of Dutch descent who offered his farm for sale on April 16, 1764.
DeKalb Avenue honors Baron Johann de Kalb, a German officer who died fighting for the Continental Army in the Revolution.
Delancey Street is named for the De Lancey family, whose large colonial estate once covered much of the Lower East Side.
The origin of the name is uncertain but may reference Edward Cornelius Delavan, a prominent temperance advocate in 19th century New York.
Delmonico Place likely takes its name from the Delmonico brothers, whose 220 acre Brooklyn farm it may once have served as a driveway.
Built in the mid 19th century to house workers constructing the nearby church, its true name may actually be Bennett Place.
Named for Elias Desbrosses, a Huguenot merchant and Trinity Church warden whose pier saw both Washington and Lincoln's body arrive.
Devoe Street preserves a family name in the Williamsburg grid west of Bushwick Avenue.
Dewey Place likely honors Admiral George Dewey, the only person ever to hold the rank of Admiral of the Navy, celebrated for his 1898 victory at Manila Bay.
Named for Dirck Dey, a Dutch soldier who arrived in New Amsterdam in 1641 and owned land from Broadway to the Hudson.
Named for the Diamond Brothers, who ran a shipyard on Greenpoint's waterfront in the 1800s.
Dikeman Street, officially named in 1835, honors John Dikeman, Brooklyn's village lawyer in 1819 who went on to become a respected judge.
Ditmars Boulevard honors Abram Ditmars, the first mayor of Long Island City, elected in 1870. His family were Dutch farmers who worked northern Queens land for generations.
Ditmars Street in Bushwick is named for the Ditmas family, Dutch settlers who farmed Brooklyn land for over two centuries.
Ditmas Avenue takes its name from Jan Jansen Van Ditmarsen Jr., a Danish patriarch who settled in Flatbush in the mid 17th century.
Division Avenue was named because it served as the dividing line between the city of Brooklyn and the town (later city) of Williamsburg.
Named for the 1765 boundary it marked between the De Lancey estate and the Rutgers farm.
Dobbin Street in Greenpoint may honor Secretary of the Navy James C. Dobbin, who purchased ships built in local Brooklyn shipyards.
Dock Street in DUMBO got its name from its original function as a working dock where ships loaded and unloaded cargo.
Dodworth Street in Bushwick likely honors the Dodworth family, famous 19th century bandmasters who helped pioneer brass band music in America.
Named for Georges Dominick, a French Huguenot refugee who became a vestryman at Trinity Church in the 1780s.
Dorchester Road was originally Avenue E before being renamed in the 1890s after the English town, part of a trend to give Brooklyn streets fancier British names.
Dorset Street in East Flatbush is named after the English county of Dorset, following a pattern of British place names in the area.
Doughty Street in Brooklyn Heights honors Charles Doughty, an 18th century lawyer who helped create the Village of Brooklyn.
Despite the spelling, Douglass Street is not named after Frederick Douglass. The origin of the name predates the abolitionist's fame.
Dover Street in Manhattan Beach is part of an alphabetical series of streets named after English places, following Amherst, Beaumont, and Coleridge.
Downing Street in Clinton Hill was laid out in 1799 and likely honors Sir George Downing, the same diplomat behind London's famous Downing Street.
Named for Edmund Driggs, the last president of the Village of Williamsburg before it was absorbed into Brooklyn.
Named for James Duane, a Revolutionary War leader and the first mayor of New York City after independence.
Dumont Avenue in Brownsville may be named for Pierre Etienne Louis Dumont, a Swiss political writer and editor of Jeremy Bentham's works.
Dunham Place honors David Dunham, the 'Father of Williamsburg' who launched the first steam ferry from Brooklyn to Manhattan.
Dupont Street carries a family name within Greenpoint's 19th century grid and later industrial landscape.
Duryea Place near the Kings Theatre in Flatbush honors the Duryea family, Huguenot settlers who arrived in Brooklyn in the 1670s.
A short Financial District lane honoring the Dutch settlers who founded New Amsterdam, Colgate started here at No. 6 in 1806.
Dyckman Street is named for the Dyckman family, Dutch farmers whose land covered much of Inwood. Their 1784 farmhouse still stands nearby as the last Dutch colonial farmhouse in Manhattan.
Dyker Place takes its name from the dikes built by 17th century Dutch settlers to drain the marshy coastal land for farming.
Eagle Street was originally just 'E Street' in Greenpoint's alphabetical grid, Ash, Box, Clay, Dupont, Eagle, Freeman...
East New York Avenue takes its name from the village of East New York, founded in 1835 by John R. Pitkin, a Connecticut businessman.
Eastern Parkway was the world's first parkway, Olmsted and Vaux coined the very term when they designed it in 1870.
Eckford Street recalls shipbuilder Henry Eckford and runs through one of Greenpoint's old industrial districts.
Eldert Street is named for the Eldert family, Dutch colonial farmers who owned large tracts in the East New York area.
Named for farmer Johannes Eldert, whose land was Lot #1 of the 47 lots granted in the 1677 charter creating New Lots.
Named in 1817 for Lt. Joseph C. Eldridge, killed in a War of 1812 ambush, later home to a landmark 1887 synagogue.
Likely named for Elizabeth Rynders, granddaughter of colonial figure Jacob Leisler, later the center of Sicilian immigrant life.
Ellery Street is named for William Ellery, a signer of the Declaration of Independence who watched each delegate sign to study their courage.
Elton Street in East New York was laid out during the neighborhood's 19th century development, likely named for a local landowner or developer.
Emerson Place honors Ralph Waldo Emerson, the Transcendentalist who famously urged Americans to trust themselves above all.
Emily Roebling Plaza honors the woman who effectively oversaw the Brooklyn Bridge's construction when her husband became bedridden.
Emmons Avenue runs along Sheepshead Bay, named for the Emmons family, who were among the area's earliest settlers and fishermen.
Empire Boulevard was originally Malbone Street, renamed after the worst subway disaster in NYC history killed 93 people there in 1918.
Engert Avenue recalls the brewing era name of George Ehret and the industrial north Brooklyn landscape around the old brewery zone.
Erasmus Street honors Desiderius Erasmus, the Dutch Renaissance humanist, his name also graces nearby Erasmus Hall, Brooklyn's oldest school.
A renamed section of Beach Street honoring John Ericsson, Swedish inventor of the Civil War ironclad USS Monitor, who lived here.
Named in 2002 for Dodgers pitcher Carl Erskine. He said having a Brooklyn street named for him beat the Hall of Fame.
Named by James DeLancey for Essex County in England, part of his pre Revolution plan for an aristocratic Delancey Square.
Etna Street in East Williamsburg takes its name from Mount Etna, the famous Sicilian volcano, reflecting the area's Italian immigrant heritage.
This East New York street honors the ancient Greek 'father of geometry', a common street name across American cities laid out in the 1800s.
Evergreen Avenue in Bushwick takes its name from its proximity to Evergreen Cemetery, which was established in 1849.
Renamed in 1827 from Garden Street after the Merchants Exchange Building was built at nearby Wall and William Streets.
Exeter Street in Manhattan Beach is part of an alphabetical A to P grid of English place names from the area's 1870s resort days.
Fair Street's name likely derives from a colonial era market or fair held in the vicinity. The street was part of Brooklyn's original village grid, predating the later numbering systems.
Falmouth Street in Manhattan Beach belongs to the alphabetical grid of English place names laid out when the area was a seaside resort.
Farragut Road honors Admiral David Farragut, who shouted 'Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!' at the Battle of Mobile Bay.
Father Capodanno Boulevard honors Vincent Capodanno, a Staten Island born Navy chaplain killed in Vietnam in 1967 while giving last rites under fire. He received the Medal of Honor posthumously.
Fayette Street likely honors the Marquis de Lafayette, the French hero of the American Revolution, whose last name was sometimes shortened to 'Fayette.'
Fenimore Street honors James Fenimore Cooper, author of 'The Last of the Mohicans', nearby streets also bear literary names.
Fillmore Avenue honors President Millard Fillmore, who signed the Compromise of 1850, a deeply controversial act that included the Fugitive Slave Law.
Fiske Place honors a local family in Park Slope. The short street features some of the neighborhood's most charming brownstones.
Flatbush Avenue follows an old Native American footpath and takes its name from the Dutch 'Vlacke Bos,' meaning flat wooded land.
Fleet Place honors Samuel Fleet, Brooklyn's postmaster and publisher, not London's Fleet Street as many assume.
Fleet Street, like nearby Fleet Place, is named for Samuel Fleet (1786 to 1864), Brooklyn's early postmaster and publisher.
Named for Benjamin Fletcher, the controversial colonial governor of New York from 1692 to 1697.
Florence Avenue in Midwood may be named for Florence, Italy, or more likely for a developer's family member, a common naming practice.
Flushing Avenue began as the Brooklyn and Newtown Turnpike and takes its name from Flushing, itself from the Dutch city of Vlissingen.
Forbell Street honors a local landowner in the East New York area, part of the street grid laid out when the neighborhood was developed.
Force Tube Avenue is named for the pressurized water main, the 'force tube', that runs beneath it, carrying Brooklyn's water supply.
Forest Avenue in the Ridgewood-Bushwick border area takes its name from the dense woodlands that once covered this part of Brooklyn and Queens.
Named for its proximity to Forest Park, the street was once considered a suburb unto itself.
Renamed in 1817 from East 2nd Street to honor Lt. Col. Benjamin Forsyth, killed in the War of 1812.
Fort Greene Place is named for Nathanael Greene, the Revolutionary War general Washington called his most gifted officer.
Fort Hamilton Parkway is named after Fort Hamilton, the gray granite fort built between 1825 and 1831 to guard the Narrows of New York Harbor. The fort itself is named after Alexander Hamilton.
Fort Washington Avenue is named for Fort Washington, the Revolutionary War fort the Continental Army built in 1776 at the highest natural point in Manhattan.
Foster Avenue honors Charles Foster, a trustee of the United Freemen's Association who helped develop the village of Greenfield (now Parkville).
Fountain Avenue in East New York was named for an actual natural spring that once flowed near its route.
Francis Lewis Boulevard honors Francis Lewis, a signer of the Declaration of Independence who lived in Whitestone. British troops later destroyed his home and imprisoned his wife in revenge.
Franklin Avenue is part of a massive 1840s street naming spree that honored 43 of the 56 Declaration of Independence signers across Brooklyn.
Franklin Street carries the name of Benjamin Franklin and became especially important once Neziah Bliss opened a public turnpike along this corridor in 1839.
Frederick Douglass Boulevard honors the escaped slave who became the most famous abolitionist in America. Central Harlem's stretch of 8th Avenue was renamed for him in 1977.
Freeman Street in Greenpoint honors James Freeman, who served as a trustee of the Village of Greenpoint in the 1850s.
Fresh Pond Road is named for a spring fed pond that once sat in Ridgewood. The pond was filled in long ago, but the road that led to it kept the name.
Front Street in DUMBO and Vinegar Hill takes its name from its position as the street fronting the East River waterfront.
Frost Street was formerly Bennett Street, renamed in 1912 for Edmund Frost, president of the Williamsburg Board of Trustees in the 1830s.
Fuller Place in Park Slope is a quiet one block street named for a local family, lined with some of the slope's prettiest brownstones.
Fulton Street is named for Robert Fulton, the engineer and inventor best known for developing commercially successful steamboat service.
Furman Street was named in 1819 for Judge William Furman, his son Gabriel wrote one of the earliest histories of Brooklyn.
Gallatin Place honors Albert Gallatin, the longest serving Treasury Secretary. He served under both Jefferson and Madison for 13 years.
Renamed in 1837 from Great Kill Road to honor Revolutionary War hero General Peter Gansevoort, grandfather of Herman Melville.
Gardner Avenue in East Williamsburg was named for a local property owner during the area's development in the mid 1800s.
Gates Avenue is named for General Horatio Gates, the Continental Army commander who won the pivotal Battle of Saratoga in 1777.
A tiny Greenwich Village lane likely named for a local family. The name long predates any LGBTQ association.
George S. Gelston turned a 1750 Revolutionary War headquarters into a grand 300 room hotel, and got an avenue named for him.
George Street in Williamsburg was likely named for a member of the British royal family, several King Georges ruled during the colonial naming era.
Gerritsen Avenue honors Wolphert Gerritsen, a Dutch settler who built a tidal mill on the creek here in the 1630s, one of Brooklyn's first.
Gerry Street is named for Elbridge Gerry, whose creative redistricting of Massachusetts gave us the word 'gerrymandering.'
Originally Baltic Avenue, renamed in 1887 after the hugely popular Glenmore Rod and Gun Club, every local politician was a member.
Glenwood Road was Avenue G before 1897, renamed with an English name as Flatbush developers continued their alphabetical rebranding.
Gold Street was named by Comfort and Joshua Sands, wealthy ropemakers who purchased 160 acres of Brooklyn waterfront land in 1784 for $12,000 and laid out the area's street grid.
Named for Abraham Gouverneur, a Huguenot merchant whose descendants include Gouverneur Morris, framer of the Constitution.
Also named for Huguenot merchant Abraham Gouverneur, often confused with a governor, but named for a merchant family.
Grafton Street's name may reference Grafton in England or the famous Grafton Street in Dublin, Ireland.
Named for brothers John and James Lorimer Graham, real estate agents who developed much of Williamsburg in the 1830s.
Grand Avenue's name reflects its intended grandeur. It was designed as a wide, tree lined boulevard in the 19th century.
Named for the Civil War general and 18th president, Grant Avenue sits near the Brooklyn-Queens border in Cypress Hills.
Grattan Street is named for Henry Grattan, the Irish patriot who won legislative independence for the Irish Parliament in 1782.
Gravesend Neck Road follows an ancient path across the 'neck' of land connecting Gravesend to Coney Island, settled by Lady Moody in 1645.
Named for lawyer Samuel Jones, "Father of the New York Bar," who insisted any street through his land bear his name.
Greene Avenue honors Nathanael Greene, the same Revolutionary War general who gives Fort Greene its name.
Originally Elm Street, renamed for Nathanael Greene, one of Washington's most trusted Revolutionary War generals.
Greenpoint Avenue takes its name directly from the neighborhood and became one of its defining east west connectors.
Named for Greenwich Village, from the Dutch "Groenwijck" meaning "Green District". It was the road to the village.
Greenwood Avenue takes its name from Green-Wood Cemetery, founded in 1838 as one of the nation's first rural cemeteries.
Renamed multiple times, from Columbia to Cozine to Burrows, it finally became Grove Street for its nearby orchards.
Guernsey Street is named for Dr. Guernsey, who started a North Brooklyn newspaper in the 1850s and later became a famous homeopathic doctor.
Guy R. Brewer Boulevard honors Guy R. Brewer, one of the first Black officials elected in Queens. New York Boulevard was renamed for him after his death in 1978.
Hale Avenue honors Nathan Hale, the Revolutionary War spy whose last words, 'I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country', became legend.
Hall Street is named for George Hall, Brooklyn's very first mayor, a painter and glazier elected in 1834.
Halleck Street honors Fitz-Greene Halleck, the poet Byron called 'the American Byron'. He was one of the most famous writers of the 1820s.
Halsey Street is named for James M. Halsey, a property owner and real estate developer when the street was laid out in 1835.
Hamilton Avenue honors Alexander Hamilton, the first Treasury Secretary, Brooklyn named many streets for Founding Fathers.
Hamilton Place also honors Alexander Hamilton, the Founding Father who established the financial system that made New York a world capital.
Hamilton Terrace is named for Alexander Hamilton, whose country home Hamilton Grange stood nearby. The founding father built the house in 1802, two years before his fatal duel with Aaron Burr.
Hammerhead Avenue inside Brooklyn Navy Yard is named for the massive 350 ton crane that once towered 25 stories over the shipyard.
Hampton Avenue's name derives from an English place name, part of the naming conventions used when the area was developed for residential use in the late 1800s.
Hancock Street honors John Hancock, whose famously oversized signature on the Declaration of Independence made his name a synonym for 'signature.'
Named in 1714 for Britain's House of Hanover when King George I took the throne. The Great Fire of 1835 broke out here.
Named for the House of Hanover, the German royal dynasty that took the British throne with King George I in 1714.
Hanson Place honors Rev. Samuel Hanson Cox, a fiery abolitionist preacher whose house was ransacked by a mob in 1834.
Harbor View Terrace's name reflects its elevated views of New York Harbor and the Narrows. It gained pop culture fame as the exterior of the Reagan family home on TV's 'Blue Bloods.'
Haring Street honors the Haring family, Dutch settlers who farmed in southern Brooklyn for generations before it was subdivided.
Harkness Avenue honors Harry Harkness, the Standard Oil heir who built the Sheepshead Bay Speedway for auto racing in 1915.
Harman Street was originally named for the Harman family, early landowners in the Bushwick area during its Dutch farming days.
Harrison Avenue honors Benjamin Harrison V of Virginia, a Declaration of Independence signer, one of 43 signers with Brooklyn streets.
Named after the Harrison Brewery, which occupied the land starting in 1765 in what is now Tribeca.
Hart Place takes its name from Hart Street, which honors John Hart, one of 43 Declaration signers given Brooklyn streets around 1846.
Hart Street honors John Hart of New Jersey, a Declaration signer whose farm was destroyed by the British in retaliation.
Harway Avenue is named for developer James Harway, but in the 1930s it swapped names with Cropsey Avenue in one of Brooklyn's oddest cartographic mysteries.
Hastings Street in East New York was part of the 1887 street renaming, likely named for the English town or the Battle of Hastings.
Hattie Jones Place honors a beloved local community leader, one of Brooklyn's many streets renamed for neighborhood activists.
Havemeyer Street preserves one of the names associated with Brooklyn's sugar refining world.
Hawthorne Street honors Nathaniel Hawthorne, author of 'The Scarlet Letter', part of Flatbush's grid of literary street names.
Hegeman Avenue honors the Hegeman family, prominent Dutch settlers and landowners in the Flatlands area of Brooklyn.
Hemlock Street in East New York is named for the hemlock tree, part of a cluster of Brooklyn streets bearing tree names.
Henderson Walk in Coney Island is named for Henry Henderson's Bathing Pavilion, once the largest on the island.
Hendrickson Place, like nearby Hendrickson Street, is named for the Hendrickson family, early Dutch settlers in the Canarsie and Flatlands areas of Brooklyn.
Hendrickson Street honors the Hendrickson family, Dutch settlers who were among the earliest landowners in southern Brooklyn.
Hendrix Place in East New York is named for the Ephraim Hendricks family, early Dutch settlers in the area.
Hendrix Street was named for the Hendrix family, early property owners in the East New York area, not the famous guitarist.
Henry Street is named for Dr. Thomas W. Henry, a prominent 1820s physician, not Patrick Henry as many assume.
The court takes its name from adjacent Herkimer Street.
Herkimer Place, like Herkimer Street, is named for Brigadier General Nicholas Herkimer (1728 to 1777), who led American forces at the Battle of Oriskany.
Herkimer Street honors Nicholas Herkimer, the general who was mortally wounded leading the militia at the Battle of Oriskany in 1777.
Herzl Street was renamed from Ames Street in 1913 to honor the father of Zionism, reflecting Brownsville's 'Little Jerusalem' era.
Named for Hester Leisler, daughter of Jacob Leisler, the colonial governor hanged for treason in 1691.
Hewes Street reflects the family name pattern that still shapes much of Williamsburg's street map.
Heyward Street honors Thomas Heyward Jr., a signer of the Declaration of Independence from South Carolina.
Hicks Street is named for the Hicks brothers, John and Jacob, who operated Brooklyn's only ferry to Manhattan in the early 1800s.
Highland Avenue takes its name from the elevated terrain of Highland Park, which sits on the glacial ridge between Brooklyn and Queens.
Highland Boulevard follows the high ridge near Highland Park, the glacial moraine that forms Brooklyn's natural spine.
Highland Place takes its name from the elevated terrain near Highland Park on Brooklyn's eastern ridge.
Hillel Place was once called Germania Place, renamed in 1959 for the ancient Jewish sage when Brooklyn College built its Hillel center.
Hillside Avenue runs along the base of the terminal moraine, the ridge of hills left by the last glacier that forms the spine of Long Island.
Himrod Street is named for Rev. J.S. Himrod, the first pastor of the South Bushwick Reformed Dutch Church founded in 1853.
Hinsdale Street in East New York was named during the 1887 renaming, likely for a local landowner or an English place name.
Homecrest Avenue takes its name from a 1900 planned suburb marketed as 'the ideal home place' by developer T.B. Ackerson.
Homecrest Court takes its name from the Homecrest neighborhood, a turn of the century planned suburban community by developer T.B. Ackerson.
Hooper Street honors William Hooper, a Declaration signer. It was originally just Eleventh Street in Williamsburg's numbered grid.
Hope Street was formerly North Street, renamed in 1885 when Williamsburg ditched its confusing numbered grid.
Hopkins Street honors Stephen Hopkins, the Rhode Island governor who signed the Declaration, one of 43 signers with Brooklyn streets.
Named for Revolutionary War General Horatio Gates, who lived on the block when it was named.
Houston Street is named for William Houstoun, a Georgia statesman and delegate to the Constitutional Convention; despite the spelling, New Yorkers pronounce it HOW-ston.
Howard Avenue honors William Howard, whose Rising Sun Tavern stood nearby. The British forced him to guide troops during the Battle of Brooklyn.
Howard Place in Windsor Terrace is named for William Howard, a partner in the Brooklyn brewing firm Howard and Fuller.
Origin debated, possibly named for fire chief Harry Howard, though the name appeared on maps before his birth.
Hoyt Avenue preserves the name of the Hoyt family, prominent early Astoria landowners whose waterfront estates stood where Astoria Park spreads today.
Hoyt Street is named for Charles Hoyt, a real estate developer who helped open up South Brooklyn in the 1830s.
Hubbard Place honors James Hubbard, one of the original 1645 patentees of Gravesend. He followed Lady Deborah Moody to Brooklyn.
Hubbard Street honors the same James Hubbard, a 1645 Gravesend patentee who fled Salem for religious freedom.
Named for Hubert Van Wagenen, a businessman connected to Trinity Church, which owned the surrounding Tribeca land.
Hudson Avenue honors Henry Hudson, the English explorer whose 1609 voyage up the river that bears his name opened New York to Dutch colonization.
Named after the Hudson River, itself named for explorer Henry Hudson who sailed it for the Dutch in 1609.
Like many Hudson named streets in New York, it references Henry Hudson, the English explorer whose 1609 voyage up the river that now bears his name opened the region to Dutch colonization.
Hull Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant was named for a local family. It sits in one of Brooklyn's most architecturally significant neighborhoods.
Humboldt Street is named for Alexander von Humboldt, the Prussian naturalist whose global reputation reached far beyond Europe.
Hunter Avenue in East New York was named for a local property owner, part of the grid laid out during the neighborhood's 19th century growth.
Hunterfly Place preserves the Dutch name 'Ander Vly' (to the swampy place), and three 1840s houses from the free Black community of Weeksville.
Huntington Street in Carroll Gardens may honor Samuel Huntington, a signer of the Declaration of Independence and President of the Continental Congress.
Huron Street was originally just H Street, likely renamed for the locally built steamship USS Huron in the 1850s.
Imlay Street was renamed in 1861 for William H. Imlay, who both sold land to the Atlantic Dock Company and held major shares in it.
Independence Avenue in Bay Ridge celebrates American independence, part of a patriotic naming cluster in the southwestern Brooklyn neighborhood.
India Street uses a global trade name that fits Greenpoint's East River and maritime context.
Ingraham Street likely honors Duncan Ingraham, the Navy officer who won a Congressional Gold Medal for rescuing a political refugee in 1853.
Irving Avenue honors Washington Irving, the author who gave America its first international literary hit with 'Rip Van Winkle.'
Irving Place also honors Washington Irving, the writer who coined 'Gotham' as a nickname for New York City.
Irvington Place likely takes its name from Irvington, the Hudson Valley village named for author Washington Irving.
Irwin Street is part of Manhattan Beach's alphabetical A to P grid of English themed street names laid out in the 1870s.
Jackie Robinson Parkway was renamed in 1997 from the Interboro Parkway to honor the baseball legend who broke the color barrier with the Brooklyn Dodgers.
Jackson Street was probably named for Daniel Jackson, a local property owner with landed interests in early Williamsburgh.
Jaffray Street is the 'J' in Manhattan Beach's A to P alphabetical grid of English themed street names.
Jamaica Avenue follows an ancient Lenape trail. Its name comes from 'Jameco,' a Native American word possibly meaning 'beaver.'
Named after St. James the Greater, the apostle. The nearby St. James Church has served the area since 1836.
Likely named for the Jaynes family who owned the land, not for a woman named Jane as many assume.
Java Street pairs with nearby India Street as part of a naming pattern that gestures beyond Brooklyn to global geography.
Jay Street honors John Jay, a founder, diplomat, and the first Chief Justice of the United States.
Jefferson Avenue honors Thomas Jefferson, the principal author of the Declaration of Independence and America's third president.
Jefferson Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant is named after Thomas Jefferson, the third U.S. president and principal author of the Declaration of Independence.
Jerome Avenue is named for Leonard Jerome, Wall Street's 'King' and investor in the Sheepshead Bay Race Track, also Winston Churchill's grandfather.
Jerome Street in East New York was likely named for the same Jerome family, prominent in New York society and real estate.
A tiny SoHo alley once called Columbian Alley, renamed around 1829, possibly for the English Channel island of Jersey.
Jewel Street in Greenpoint belongs to a cluster of streets named for precious materials, Gem, Diamond, and Ruby streets are nearby.
Named for John Haberdinck, a Dutch shoemaker who owned the Shoemakers Field the street crossed.
Johnson Avenue honors Jeremiah Johnson, Brooklyn's third mayor who served for 40 years as town supervisor.
Johnson Street honors the Johnson family estate, Rev. Evan Johnson developed it as an upper middle class enclave in the 1830s.
Named for Dr. Gardiner Jones, who laid out this Greenwich Village lane in 1794, his in law got "Great Jones Street."
Joralemon Street honors Teunis Joralemon, the farmer whose orchard covered the land where this Brooklyn Heights street now runs.
Judge Street in Williamsburg is a small street whose namesake remains uncertain, possibly named for a local magistrate.

Jumel Terrace is named for Eliza Jumel and the Morris Jumel Mansion, the oldest house in Manhattan. Eliza rose from poverty to become one of the richest women in America and briefly married Aaron Burr.
Junction Boulevard is named for the line it marks, the old junction between the separate communities of Corona and Jackson Heights, and later the Queens borough boundary of two districts.
Junius Street in Brownsville may nod to ancient Rome. The Junii were a famous clan whose most notorious member helped overthrow a king.
Kane Street in Carroll Gardens honors John K. Kane, a Brooklyn civic leader. It's also home to the oldest continuously operating synagogue in Brooklyn.
Karweg Place in Gravesend is named for the Karweg family, early Dutch settlers who farmed the area.
Keap Street preserves a family name from Brooklyn's older landholding and mercantile world.
Kenilworth Place takes its name from Kenilworth Castle in England, part of Flatbush's tradition of borrowing English place names.
Named in 1911 by politician "Big Tim" Sullivan for his mother's hometown of Kenmare in County Kerry, Ireland.
Kenmore Terrace in Flatbush is named for Kenmore, the Fredericksburg plantation home of George Washington's sister.
Kensington Street is named for the London borough, fitting for a Brooklyn neighborhood that borrowed its name from the same royal district.
Kent Avenue is named for Edward Augustus Kent and traces Williamsburg's old industrial East River waterfront.
Kent Street in Greenpoint was originally K Street, renamed for James Kent, the influential New York jurist known as 'the American Blackstone.'
Kermit Place in Midwood is named for Kermit Roosevelt, Theodore Roosevelt's adventurous son who explored Brazil and fought in both World Wars.
Kimball Street is part of Manhattan Beach's alphabetical grid of streets laid out in the 1870s by developer Austin Corbin.
Named for Rufus King, Founding Father and U.S. Senator from New York, not for any British monarch.
Kingsland Avenue preserves an old family name on Greenpoint's eastern industrial edge near Newtown Creek.
Kingston Avenue in Crown Heights is named after Kingston, New York, the Ulster County seat that briefly served as New York's state capital in 1777 before the British burned it.
Kissena Boulevard takes its name from Kissena Lake, which nurseryman Samuel Parsons named with a Chippewa word meaning it is cold.
Knapp Street in Sheepshead Bay honors Shepherd Knapp, a 19th century NYC banker and philanthropist who served as president of the Mechanics' Bank.
Knickerbocker Avenue takes its name from Washington Irving's fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, the character who gave all New Yorkers their nickname.
Korean War Veterans Plaza in Downtown Brooklyn was dedicated in 2002, one of the few NYC spaces honoring the 'Forgotten War.'
Kosciuszko Street in Bed-Stuy honors Tadeusz Kosciuszko (1746 to 1817), a Polish military engineer who sailed to America in 1776 to fight in the Revolutionary War.
Kossuth Place honors Lajos Kossuth, the Hungarian freedom fighter who drew massive NYC crowds during his 1851 American tour.
Kouwenhoven Lane preserves the name of one of Brooklyn's founding Dutch families. The Kouwenhovens settled New Utrecht in the 1650s.
Lafayette Street honors the Marquis de Lafayette, the French aristocrat who became a hero of the American Revolution.
Lafayette Walk honors the Marquis de Lafayette, the French hero of the American Revolution who received a wild Brooklyn reception on his 1824 return visit.
Named for William Laight, a Trinity Church vestryman and ardent anti Royalist during the American Revolution.
Lake Street in Gravesend takes its name from the small freshwater lakes that once dotted the low lying marshlands of southern Brooklyn.
Lancaster Avenue in Brownsville may honor the Pennsylvania city, or the English House of Lancaster associated with the Wars of the Roses.
Langham Street is the 'L' in Manhattan Beach's A to P alphabetical grid, named for the Langham Hotel, a grand London landmark.
Laurel Avenue is one of several tree named streets in southern Brooklyn, a common 19th century naming convention for new developments.
Lawrence Avenue likely honors Captain James Lawrence, the War of 1812 naval hero whose dying words were 'Don't give up the ship.'
Lawrence Street in Downtown Brooklyn is named for Charles K. Lawrence, son in law of Dr. John Duffield, both men have streets steps apart.
Williamsburg's streets honor Declaration signers, Lee Avenue is named for Virginia's Lee brothers, who helped launch American independence.
Named for the Lefferts family, Dutch settlers who once owned most of what became Crown Heights and Bed-Stuy.
Lefferts Boulevard honors the Lefferts family, Dutch landowners whose farms stretched across colonial Queens and Brooklyn before the street grid.
Lefferts Place in Clinton Hill is named for the prominent Dutch Lefferts family, who owned most of modern day Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights North.
Lenox Avenue honors James Lenox, the bibliophile whose vast book collection helped found the New York Public Library. In Harlem it is co named Malcolm X Boulevard.
Lenox Road in Flatbush was likely named for James Lenox, the wealthy bibliophile whose collection helped found the New York Public Library.
Named for Samuel Leonard, a school superintendent who built Williamsburg's P.S. 34.
Named for shipping merchant Jacob Le Roy, though a romantic legend ties it to the lost son of Louis XVI hiding in New York.
Named for Morgan Lewis, Revolutionary War veteran and Governor of New York from 1804 to 1807.
This Bed-Stuy street echoes the Revolutionary War, named for the 1775 Battle of Lexington, the 'shot heard round the world.'
Liberty Avenue wasn't named for patriotism. It was the free road, while Jamaica Avenue and Rockaway Boulevard charged tolls.
Renamed from Crown Street in 1793 to celebrate American liberty after the Revolution.
One of several Brooklyn streets honoring President Lincoln. This Cypress Hills road winds through a neighborhood built up in the 1880s.
Lincoln Place got its name after an 1873 murder so scandalous that neighbors petitioned to rename the street.
Lincoln Road in Prospect Lefferts Gardens was once called East New York Avenue, likely renamed around 1873 for President Lincoln.
Linden Street became Bushwick's first ever historic district in 2023, honoring its remarkably intact 1880s 1900s rowhouses.
Named for the Lispenard family, whose farm and meadows covered a swath of lower Manhattan starting in 1746.
Named for Philip Livingston, the only signer of the Declaration of Independence from Brooklyn, and a man with a complicated legacy.
Livonia Avenue was originally named for the Linningtons, a local farming family, before being renamed for a faraway Baltic province.
Formerly Locust Street, Logan Street was renamed in 1887 for the Civil War general who created Memorial Day.
This short Greenpoint street is named for the Lombardy region of Italy, in a neighborhood shaped by generations of Italian immigrants.
Named for James Lorimer Graham, a developer who with his brother sold building lots across 1830s Williamsburg.
Lott Avenue in Brownsville honors the Lott family, Dutch settlers who farmed Flatlands for over 200 years.
Lott Street also honors the Lott family, whose 1720 farmhouse in Marine Park is one of Brooklyn's oldest surviving buildings.
Named for the colonial couples who strolled this Brooklyn Heights lane on summer evenings.
Named for Augustus C. Ludlow, a U.S. naval lieutenant who died a hero in the War of 1812.
Luquer Street in Carroll Gardens honors Nicholas Luquer, a prominent 19th century Brooklyn civic leader and banker.
Lynch Street in Williamsburg was named for Thomas Lynch Jr., a South Carolina signer of the Declaration of Independence.
MacDonough Street honors Commodore Thomas Macdonough, whose 1814 victory at Lake Champlain saved New York from British invasion.
MacDougal Street in Brooklyn honors Alexander McDougall, the Scottish born Sons of Liberty leader who was jailed for criticizing the British.
Named for Alexander McDougall, a Scottish born Son of Liberty jailed by the British for a seditious pamphlet in 1770.
Mackay Place is one of Manhattan Beach's alphabetically ordered streets laid out by developer Austin Corbin in the 1870s.
Macon Street in Bed-Stuy was named for Nathaniel Macon, a North Carolina congressman who served as Speaker of the House.
Named in 1826 after James Madison, the fourth U.S. president, a decade before Madison Avenue opened nearby.
Main Street in DUMBO marks the site of the original Brooklyn ferry landing, the spot where Brooklyn was born.
Named for Ralph Malbone, a grocer who farmed the surrounding land in the early 1800s.
Malcolm X Boulevard was renamed from Reid Avenue in 1985 to honor the civil rights leader who was a powerful voice in Brooklyn.
Manhattan Avenue takes its name from the island across the East River, signaling the commercial pull Manhattan exerted on Greenpoint's growth.
Maple Street in Prospect-Lefferts Gardens is one of several tree named streets radiating from Prospect Park.
Marconi Place honors Guglielmo Marconi, the Italian inventor who won the Nobel Prize for pioneering wireless telegraphy.
Marcus Garvey Boulevard was renamed from Sumner Avenue in 1987 to honor the Jamaican born Black nationalist leader.
Marcy Avenue is named for William L. Marcy, the NY governor who coined the phrase 'to the victor belong the spoils.'
Marine Avenue in Bay Ridge takes its name from its proximity to the waterfront along the Narrows, the strait between Brooklyn and Staten Island.
Marion Street was named for Francis Marion, the 'Swamp Fox' of the American Revolution who pioneered guerrilla warfare.
Originally George Street (for King George III), it was renamed in 1813 after the nearby Catherine Market.
Named from the Dutch "Marcktveldt" for New Amsterdam's first cattle market, established nearby in 1641.
Marlborough Road in Flatbush was named for the Duke of Marlborough, part of the English themed street names in Victorian era Flatbush.
Marshall Street in Bushwick likely honors John Marshall, the longest serving Chief Justice who established judicial review.
Named for one of Flatbush's original Dutch settler families. The Martenses have been Brooklyn landowners since the 1600s.
This tiny Bed-Stuy block became the first street in all of NYC named for Dr. King back in 1974.
Named for the Mespeatches, a Lenape sub tribe, the word likely means 'at the bad water place' for the area's swampy terrain.
Originally called Remsen Street, Maujer Street was renamed in 1937 for Daniel Maujer, a local alderman and landowner.
Once called Gravesend Avenue, McDonald Avenue was controversially renamed in 1933 for a beloved Brooklyn court clerk.
McGuinness Boulevard is named for Peter J. McGuinness, a Brooklyn politician and civic figure associated with Irish-American public life in the borough.
Meadow Street in East Williamsburg is a descriptive street name likely referencing the open meadows and grasslands that existed in the area before urbanization.
Meeker Avenue is named for the Meeker family and became a major connector on Greenpoint's southern edge.
Once called Ralph Street, Menahan Street was renamed for Patrick J. Menahan, a corset manufacturer who had his shop right on the block.
Mercer Street honors Revolutionary War general Hugh Mercer and later became part of SoHo's cast iron district.
Folk legend Woody Guthrie lived at 3520 Mermaid Avenue from 1943, inspiring the Billy Bragg and Wilco album named after the street.
Merrick Boulevard carries the name of the Merrick, a Lenape people of western Long Island whose name also marks the old road toward the town of Merrick.
Meserole Avenue carries the Meserole family name and runs through one of Greenpoint's old industrial residential edges.
Named for one of Greenpoint's founding families, Jean Miserol, a French Huguenot, arrived in New Amsterdam in 1663.
Named for Arthur Middleton of South Carolina, one of the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence.
Midwood Street's name comes from the Dutch 'Midwout' meaning 'middle woods'. It sat in the forest halfway between Bushwick and Brooklyn.
A quiet East New York street. Its name may reference the English town of Milford but the exact origin is undocumented.
Named for the colonial era tidal mills that ground grain using the power of Jamaica Bay's rising and falling tides.
Mill Street's name reflects Brooklyn's agricultural past, when water powered or tidal mills dotted the waterfront landscape.
Named for Horace A. Miller, a 19th century builder who helped develop East New York after its original developer went bust.
Named for 1840s ship chandler Daniel Milton. This Greenpoint street is famous for its gorgeous row of historic houses.
Named for Minetta Creek, from the Lenape "manette" (devil water), filtered through Dutch as "Mintje Kill" (little stream).
Minetta Street takes its name from the buried Minetta Creek, whose winding course its curved path still traces.
Moffat Street in Bushwick was likely named for a local landowner. The Moffat family held property in the area.
Monitor Street takes its name from the USS Monitor, the ironclad warship built nearby in Greenpoint.
Monroe Place in Brooklyn Heights honors James Monroe, the fifth president whose 'Monroe Doctrine' warned Europe away from the Americas.
Monroe Street in Bed-Stuy also honors President James Monroe, part of Brooklyn's tradition of naming streets for Founding Fathers.
Montague Street honors Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who famously brought smallpox inoculation from Turkey to England.
Montgomery Place in Park Slope is one of Brooklyn's most beautiful blocks, named for the general who died storming Quebec in 1775.
Montgomery Street also honors General Richard Montgomery, the first American general killed in the Revolution.
The definitive origin of its name is lost to history. Speculative theories include a reference to the Duke of Montrose or Sir Walter Scott's novel, but neither has been confirmed.
Moore Street in Bushwick was named for a local landowner. The Moore family held property in the area during its colonial era.
Originally called Beaver Lane, this Financial District street likely honors the prominent colonial Morris family of New York.
Most likely named for Jacob Morton, a Revolutionary era militia general and prominent New York civic leader.
Renamed in 1982 for community activist Frank Mosco; it was formerly Cross Street at the heart of the Five Points.
Mother Gaston Boulevard was renamed from Stone Avenue in 1988 to honor Rosetta 'Mother' Gaston, a tireless Brownsville community activist.
Mott Street preserves the name of the Mott family and later became one of the defining streets of Chinatown and old Five Points Manhattan.
Moultrie Street honors General William Moultrie, the Revolutionary War hero whose palmetto log fort gave South Carolina its nickname.
Mulberry Street likely preserves an early landscape name, recalling mulberry trees that once grew in the area before dense urban development took over.
Named for Robert Murray, the Scottish merchant whose wife Mary famously stalled British officers during the Revolution.
Myrtle Avenue was named for the myrtle trees once plentiful in the area and first laid out in 1835.
Narrows Avenue takes its name from the Narrows, the tidal strait between Brooklyn and Staten Island that guards New York Harbor.
Nassau Avenue carries a Dutch dynastic name and became one of Greenpoint's main east west corridors.
Named by 1696 for the Dutch House of Orange-Nassau; in the 19th century it became New York's Newspaper Row.
Navy Street takes its name from the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which it borders. The yard was established in 1801 and built some of the Navy's most famous ships.
Neilson Street in Carroll Gardens may honor John Neilson, a New Jersey patriot who fought at the Battle of Brooklyn.
Nelson Street in Carroll Gardens may honor Admiral Horatio Nelson, the British naval hero of Trafalgar, or a local family.
Neptune Avenue is one of Coney Island's three major east west thoroughfares, named after Neptune, the Roman god of the sea.
Nevins Street is named for Russell Nevins, who with Charles Hoyt bought up much of what is now Boerum Hill in the 1830s.
New Dorp Lane preserves the Dutch name Nieuw Dorp, meaning new village, the settlement founded around 1671 after the island's original Oude Dorp, or old village, near South Beach.
New Jersey Avenue in East New York honors the Garden State, one of several state named streets in the area.
So named because it was the first street added after the British took over New Amsterdam in 1664.
New Utrecht literally means 'New Old Fort', Utrecht derives from Dutch words meaning 'old fort,' named for a homesick Dutch colonist in 1655.
New York Avenue in Crown Heights honors the state itself, and runs through one of Brooklyn's most culturally vibrant neighborhoods.
Newkirk Avenue honors the Newkirk family, Dutch settlers whose farm once occupied the Flatbush area.
Newport Street in Brownsville likely takes its name from Newport, either the Rhode Island city or an English town.
Newtown Road is an old path toward the colonial town of Newtown, the English settlement of 1652 that is now Elmhurst.
Nichols Avenue in East New York was likely named for a local family. The Nichols held property in the area.
Norfolk Street also carries an English county name, fitting the old Lower East Side pattern of borrowed place names.
North 6 Street is part of the numbered street system laid out during Williamsburg's 19th century north side expansion.
North 7 Street belongs to Williamsburg's numbered street grid, created as the village expanded beyond its original waterfront core.
Named in 1790 for Bishop Benjamin Moore, president of Columbia College and father of Clement Clarke Moore.
Northern Boulevard is named for its place in the road system, the northern of the main routes running east across Queens and into Long Island.
The street's naming origin is not well documented; the name may derive from 'north woods' or possibly from an early landowner.
Nostrand Avenue is named for the Dutch settler family of Hans Hansen Von Norstrand, who arrived in Flatbush in 1638.
Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1860s, Ocean Parkway was named because the road led from Prospect Park to the ocean at Coney Island.
Old Fulton Street is named for the historic Fulton Ferry connection that tied Brooklyn to Manhattan before the Brooklyn Bridge transformed regional travel.
Named for an old ship slip; a man made inlet where boats docked on the East River before it was filled in.
Named for Oliver De Lancey, a British loyalist brigadier exiled to England after the Revolution.
Onderdonk Avenue honors the Onderdonk family, Dutch farmers of Ridgewood. Their 1709 fieldstone house nearby is the oldest Dutch colonial stone house in New York City.
Orchard Street remembers the orchard on the old De Lancey estate and later became a defining Lower East Side immigrant corridor.
Park Lane is named for Forest Park, the wooded Queens preserve it borders on the Kew Gardens side.
Park Lane South is named for Forest Park, forming the wooded park's southern boundary through Woodhaven.
The street's name reflects the 19th century practice of naming streets for nearby parkland to attract residential development.
Renamed in 1886 from Chatham Street because it faces City Hall Park; it became famous as "Newspaper Row."
Parkside Avenue existed on paper as 'Robinson Street' before being renamed in 1902 to advertise its location right on the park's edge.
Parsons Boulevard honors the Parsons family of nurserymen, whose Flushing tree nursery planted much of the city. Samuel Parsons Jr. went on to become the parks commissioner of New York.
Named for Aaron Patchin, a surveyor who married the landowner's daughter, E.E. Cummings and Djuna Barnes later lived here.
Pearl Street's name refers to the oyster and shell deposits once found there, making it a rare street whose name preserves both landscape and deep colonial history.
Named for Johannes (Jan) Peck, an early Dutch settler who emigrated from the Netherlands before 1650.
Named for the Pell family, Thomas Pell signed a 1654 treaty with the Siwanoy for 50,000 acres of what became the Bronx.
Pennsylvania Avenue is part of a cluster of state named streets in East New York, you can also walk down Alabama, Georgia, and Vermont nearby.
Named for Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry, hero of the 1813 Battle of Lake Erie during the War of 1812.
Named for explorer Zebulon Pike of Pike's Peak fame, who was killed fighting the British in 1813.
Originally King Street in the colonial era, renamed after the Revolution for a pine grove on a nearby Dutch farm.
Named in 1834 for merchant Jacob Platt, through whose property the two block Financial District street was extended.
President Street is part of a civic minded naming pattern, nearby you'll find Union, Congress, and Carroll Streets honoring American ideals.
Derived from the Dutch "Princess Straet", one of the few royal street names to survive the post Revolution purge.
Originally called 'Middle Street,' it was renamed by the New York Legislature in 1868 to celebrate the brand new Prospect Park next door.
Queens Boulevard carries the name of the borough, which honors Catherine of Braganza, the Portuguese queen of King Charles II, when Queens County was created in 1683.
Ralph Patchen was so prominent that Brooklyn named two streets after him, Ralph Avenue uses his first name, Patchen Avenue his last.
Named for Joseph Reade, a colonial warden of Trinity Church, also half the namesake of the Duane Reade pharmacy chain.
Named for its proximity to Trinity Church, referring to the office of the church's rector rather than a specific person.
Richmond Terrace carries Staten Island's colonial name. Richmond County was named in 1683 for Charles Lennox, Duke of Richmond, an illegitimate son of King Charles II.
Ridge Street likely recalls the old topography of Manhattan's east side before the island was fully graded and leveled.
Riverside Drive takes its name from the Hudson River it overlooks and Riverside Park beside it, both designed by Frederick Law Olmsted in the 1870s.
Rivington Street is named for James Rivington, the controversial Loyalist printer and publisher of the Royal Gazette during the Revolutionary era.
Named from the Lenape word 'Reckowacky,' likely meaning 'sandy place', one of NYC's most persistent Indigenous place names.
Rockaway Boulevard points toward the Rockaways, whose name comes from the Lenape word Reckouwacky, often read as place of sands.
Roebling Street recalls the bridge building family behind some of Brooklyn's most famous suspension spans.
Roosevelt Avenue honors President Theodore Roosevelt, the New York born reformer and outdoorsman. The Corona and Jackson Heights corridor was named for him when it opened in 1917.
Named for Henry Rutgers, a Revolutionary War captain whose estate covered much of the Lower East Side.
Named in 1835 for the Revolutionary War Battles of Saratoga, the turning point that brought France into the war.
Named for Colonel Alexander Scammell, Washington's Adjutant General, mortally wounded by British dragoons at Yorktown.
Schermerhorn Street honors Abraham Schermerhorn, a wealthy merchant from a Dutch family that settled New York in 1636.
Like many nearby streets, it preserves a family name while the surrounding blocks reflect later industrial and residential growth.
Named for the Seneca people of the Iroquois League, one of several Brooklyn area streets honoring Native American nations.
Likely named for Colonel Marinus Willett, Sheriff of New York from 1784 to 1788, who later became mayor.
Skillman Avenue honors the Skillman family, Dutch settlers who farmed the Sunnyside and Long Island City land for generations before the street grid arrived.
Smith Street preserves a common early Brooklyn family name and later became one of downtown Brooklyn's mixed commercial corridors.
The street was later renamed William after Willem Beekman, who arrived in New Amsterdam in 1647 with Peter Stuyvesant.
Named for an actual freshwater spring that ran through Lispenard's Meadow. Its underground stream still floods basements today.
Originally George Street for King George III, one of eight George Streets renamed after the Revolution.
Originally New Bowery, renamed in 1947 for the nearby St. James Roman Catholic Church, built in 1837 for Irish immigrants.
Named in 1835 after the fashionable St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery to attract wealthy buyers to new townhouses.
Stanton Street is named for one of the old landowning families whose names survive in the Lower East Side street map.
Origin debated, possibly named for "staple" goods unloaded at nearby markets, or for landowner John J. Staples circa 1800.
Originally Copsey Street after the Lenape village of Kopsee, renamed for the State House built on the site of old Fort Amsterdam.

Steinway Street is named for Henry Steinway and his piano firm Steinway and Sons, which built a complete company town in northern Astoria in the 1870s with its own factory, housing, church, and trolley line.
Named for settler Nicholas Stillwell, whose 1640s farm launched a dynasty. The original Nathan's hot dog stand sits at Stillwell and Surf.
Named for its cobblestones; in 1658 it became the first paved street in New Amsterdam.
St. Nicholas Avenue honors Saint Nicholas, the patron saint the Dutch brought to New Amsterdam. Much of the avenue follows the old Wickquasgeck trail, a Native American path older than the grid.
Named for Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director general of New Netherland, whose farm the street once crossed.
Suffolk Street carries an English county name, part of a broader naming pattern on Manhattan's east side.
Named in 1799 for Major General John Sullivan, who fought at Trenton, Brandywine, and Germantown in the Revolution.
Sutphin Boulevard honors John H. Sutphin, a Jamaica banker and ten term Queens county clerk who donated land near the new railroad station that the boulevard now serves.
Named for Peter D. Sutter, a powerful 19th century Brooklyn Democratic boss, local politics literally put on the map.
Union Avenue commemorates the 1835 joining of the villages of Williamsburgh and Bushwick, running through the heart of the area their merger created.
Not a Civil War reference, Union Street is named for the Union Stores, massive 1800s warehouses that stored sugar and molasses on the Red Hook docks.
Utica Avenue was named in 1835 for the upstate city of Utica, part of a wave of Brooklyn streets honoring Erie Canal towns.
Van Siclen Avenue is named for one of the first Dutch families to settle on Long Island in the 17th century.
Vernon Boulevard is named for British Admiral Edward Vernon, the same namesake as Mount Vernon. George Washington's half brother Lawrence served under Vernon at sea and brought the name to America.
Wadsworth Avenue honors General James S. Wadsworth, a Union commander and opponent of slavery who was killed leading troops at the Battle of the Wilderness in 1864.
Wall Street takes its name from the defensive wall the Dutch built across northern New Amsterdam in 1653.
Welling Court honors the Welling family, Astoria landowners who lived here as early as the 1700s. The little lane is now famous for its open air mural project.
Hamburg Avenue became Wilson Avenue in honor of President Woodrow Wilson. The old name survives carved into the stonework of several corner buildings.
Winthrop Street sits in a Flatbush area where developers named streets after famous American literary and historical figures to attract buyers.
Withers Street is named for Reuben Withers, a 19th century merchant and ferry investor connected to the growth of north Brooklyn.
Woodhaven Boulevard takes its name from the Woodhaven neighborhood it crosses. The road itself began as South Meadow Road in 1668, a path villagers used to reach Jamaica Bay grazing meadows.
Woodside Avenue is named for the Woodside neighborhood, itself named in the 1860s for the wooded estate and newspaper columns of local writer John Kelsey.
Wythe Avenue is named for George Wythe, a Virginia jurist, Declaration signer, and one of the early republic's most respected legal educators.
York Street honors the same Duke of York who gave New York its name when the British seized the colony from the Dutch in 1664.
